name: PT Adaro Andalan Indonesia Tbk

frontmatter.title: Adaro Andalan Indonesia — a first-quartile coal producer the market now prices at our through-cycle NAV
frontmatter.summary: AADI is a first-quartile-cost Indonesian thermal coal producer with a net-cash balance sheet and a monetised Australian asset. This refresh re-underwrites every key input: the royalty is the rate the audited accounts show being paid, volume holds the company's own flat plan, costs hold the last actual, and the Kestrel proceeds sit in the valuation bridge. On our corrected through-cycle NAV the shares are no longer expensive; we move to BUY, target Rp12,399.
thesis: AADI sells lower-CV thermal coal into a largely domestic and PLTU customer base, so its realised price sits well below the Newcastle marker the market capitalises; the realised ratio is calibrated on the last actual, to the benchmark that prices the product, and held flat — the grade wedge widens inside the bear's price leg rather than being assumed away.

The royalty convention is now the one the audited accounts show being paid [F20] rather than the statutory IUPK band, applied end to end, so the model reproduces FY2025A EBITDA at FY2025A prices and volume instead of over-charging the state take. That single correction is the largest reason the through-cycle NAV moves.

Volume holds the company's own plan at the FY2025 record of 71.9 Mt rather than the prior round's unsourced drift to a level far below it, and strip ratio and unit costs hold the last actual; the ex-Kestrel reserve base supports the window at that rate, so this is the reserve life, not a growth assumption.

The balance sheet is net cash and the Kestrel divestment has delivered 700.0 million dollars of net proceeds after the 30 June balance-sheet date — carried in the valuation bridge — funding a buyback authorised at up to IDR5.00tn and a step-up FY2026E dividend paid out of operating free cash flow of about US$1,332.6m [S2][S3].

Our reverse cash flow says the market price implies a Newcastle benchmark of about 120.8 dollars a tonne — roughly the deck's own forward path — so the equity is priced at our through-cycle value rather than at a war premium in perpetuity. The bull case, a premium that persists, still adds duration and is argued in full; the bear is mirrored on the same three drivers.

blocks.text: **What changed and why.** This refresh re-underwrites every key input under the house's "most likely, never most cautious" policy, and the changes are to our model, not to the company's operating record. Four of them matter [S15]. First, the royalty convention: the prior round charged the statutory IUPK band rate on top of a cost base built from the rate AADI actually pays, a mixed convention the pilot review named as an error; we now apply the rate the audited accounts show being paid, 14.2% of revenue, consistently. The engine's calibration gate confirms the repair: at the FY2025A benchmark and the FY2025A volume the model now reproduces FY2025A EBITDA instead of over-charging the state take and understating the year. Second, volume: the prior round drifted sales from 71.9 Mt down to a level far below the plan with no source; volume now holds the FY2025 record and the company's own FY2026 plan flat across the window, which the ex-Kestrel reserve base supports as the mine life. Third, costs: the strip ratio and the unit-cost residual no longer creep upward unsourced — both hold the last actual. Fourth, the 700.0 million dollars of Kestrel net proceeds received in October 2026, after the balance-sheet date, are now in the valuation bridge. The method, the through-cycle Newcastle benchmark, the calibrated realisation and the reserve-derived horizon are unchanged [S15]. The rating moves with the value: BUY.

We carry coverage of PT Adaro Andalan Indonesia Tbk, the thermal-coal arm spun out of Alamtri Resources (formerly Adaro Energy) and listed in late 2024, at BUY with a twelve-month target of Rp12,399 against a last price of Rp11,375 — an expected total return of 30.7% including the modelled dividend stream [S4][S10].

The variant view is now about *how the market is pricing the reserve, not whether it is expensive*. AADI is a genuinely good coal business: first-quartile unit cash costs of roughly 41.1 dollars per tonne, an owned barging and transshipment chain, a net cash balance sheet, and a demonstrated willingness to distribute cash [S10][S13]. It is not a Newcastle producer, and we do not price it as one: its realised price runs far below the six-thousand kcal/kg marker because it sells lower-CV thermal coal, mostly to domestic and PLTU customers, with roughly a quarter of volumes exposed to the standing domestic price cap [S15][S13]. The model that gets this name right is a life-of-asset cash flow at the house deck's through-cycle price, not a multiple on peak-cycle earnings — and on that cash flow the equity is fairly to modestly cheaply valued rather than expensive.

On the house coal deck's own path — spot 150.3 dollars per tonne easing to 105.0 long-run — our primary method gives Rp11,812 per share against a price of Rp11,375. The reverse cash flow is the cleanest way to see the change: the price now implies a Newcastle benchmark of about 120.8 dollars per tonne, roughly 1.0 times the deck's FY2027E level and far below the deck's spot print — the market is capitalising the deck's own forward path, not a war premium in perpetuity [S2][S15]. What the low headline multiples show is cycle position rather than value: the forward P/E of 3.9x, the modelled dividend yield of 21.7% on a trailing dividend base of Rp1,001.4 per share and the FCFE yield of 25.5% are computed on a forecast year the deck says is above the long run, so they must be read against the through-cycle NAV, not instead of it [S0].

The bull case is real and is argued in full in the scenario section: a war premium that persists, RKAB discipline that holds Indonesian supply tight, and the company executing on its cost base would carry the equity well above our base value, and the operating leverage of a thin-margin producer makes that a large move. Add the barging chain that defends the cost quartile and the North Kalimantan generation build, which absorbed 243.0 million dollars of capex to the nine-month mark and funds industrial demand in Kalimantan [S13]. We do not, however, assume any of that as the base path, and we assume no product re-rating, because none is sourced: the base case reproduces the last actual year's economics at the deck's own prices. Weighing a mirrored bull and bear around a base that sits at today's price, we rate BUY.

Three things move the value: the Newcastle path and how AADI's realised discount behaves against it; Indonesian supply discipline through RKAB quotas; and the pace at which the Kestrel cash is returned to shareholders rather than reinvested domestically [S2][S3][S13].

PT Adaro Andalan Indonesia Tbk is an Indonesian thermal-coal producer and coal-supply-chain operator, headquartered in Jakarta and listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange since December 2024 [S4][S10]. The company sits inside the Adaro group controlled by Garibaldi "Boy" Thohir, and was separated from Alamtri Resources Indonesia (ADRO) in a spin-off; ADRO was AADI's parent before the separation [S3]. It reports in US dollars, which aligns its revenue with the coal price it sells against and removes a layer of rupiah translation noise from the operating line [S10].

The operating core is Indonesian thermal coal mining. Sales volume has grown from the low sixties of megatonnes in the early part of the decade to 68.1 Mt in FY2024, with production of 65.8 Mt in the same year and FY2025 sales of 71.9 Mt, both ahead of target [S15][S10]. Management's own plan for FY2026 targets sales at least as high as that level, and we hold FY2026E at 71.9 Mt [S15][S5]. The company hedges its geological risk with a conservative strip ratio: the reported actual strip ratio was 4.3 times in FY2024 and management guided 4.3 times for FY2025, with overburden removal of 286.0 million bank cubic metres in FY2024 [S10][S13].

Around the mining core sits a vertically integrated logistics and services business that the company describes as covering coal barging and transshipment, fuel-oil transportation and management, river channel management and dredging, multipurpose terminal and stockpile management, stevedoring and shipyard operations, plus water supply and treatment and power-plant leasing [S10]. This matters for two reasons. First, owning the barging chain captures a margin that peers pay away to third parties, and it is a meaningful part of why AADI's delivered cost sits in the first quartile. Second, the company is building power generation to support industrial activity in North Kalimantan, funded from a capital programme that had absorbed 243.0 million dollars by the nine-month mark of FY2025 against a full-year budget in the low hundreds of millions [S13]. We describe this as a capex-funded industrial-support activity on the company's own disclosure, not as a contracted earnings stream: the annual report's own segment note shows the electricity-asset-rental segment carrying essentially no external revenue yet, so we credit no lease earnings — and the one press source that quantified them was broker research and has been removed from the basis as contaminated [S15].

Geographically the business is Indonesian-centred after the Australian disposal. The largest single market is Indonesia itself, followed by India, Malaysia and China, and the customer base is predominantly power plants and other end users [S15]. The flagship product is Envirocoal, a medium-calorific thermal coal in the 4,000 kcal/kg to 5,000 kcal/kg band with ultra-low ash, sulphur and nitrogen content [S15]. That product and customer mix is the single most important fact about this company's price realisation, and we return to it in the industry section below.

The group also held a large Australian metallurgical coal position — Kestrel Coal — acquired to diversify production outside Indonesia [S6]. The company agreed to sell the stake for an upfront cash consideration of about 1,850.0 million dollars plus a maximum contingent element of about 550.0 million dollars payable annually over five years after completion, and completed the transfer to Yancoal in October 2026, receiving approximately 700.0 million dollars after tax [S2][S6]. The headline upfront and the net receipt reconcile: the former is the pre-tax, pre-adjustment SPA consideration, while the latter is the cash actually received via Adaro Capital after tax and closing adjustments. Management framed the disposal as consistent with a business focus shifting back to domestic development, and earmarked the proceeds for domestic expansion, dividends and partial repayment of group borrowings [S2].

Thermal coal is a commodity business, so the industry analysis that matters is price formation, cost-curve position and the regulatory wedge between the world price and the Indonesian realised price. Each of those cuts against the market's apparent read on AADI [S15][S13].

Start with price. The house coal deck carries Newcastle six-thousand kcal/kg thermal coal at a spot of 150.3 dollars per tonne, easing through the forecast to a long-run 105.0 dollars per tonne. The deck's reasoning is that the current bid reflects a war premium plus Chinese supply discipline — mine-safety curbs and output declines — and Indonesian quota cuts and drought disruption, and that this normalises as Chinese mines restart, Indonesia relaxes production above its national target and Indian and Vietnamese demand reverts [S15][S12]. That is a mean-reversion view, and it is the view we are paid to underwrite rather than the spot tape.

Now the realisation wedge, which is where the market most visibly misprices this name. The Indonesian reference price system is not Newcastle. The government sets a Harga Batubara Acuan — a high-CV reference on a six-thousand-three-hundred kcal/kg basis — twice monthly, and it has functioned as an export pricing floor since early 2025, with the latest print around 126.8 dollars per tonne, materially below the Newcastle marker [S14][S15]. Domestic power-sector sales are subject to a standing price cap carried in the deck at 70.0 dollars per tonne [S6][S15]. For a producer whose largest market is Indonesia and whose customers are overwhelmingly power plants, the realised price is anchored to the HBA complex and the domestic cap, and the model captures that wedge as a persistent discount to the Newcastle marker. The realisation ratio is calibrated on the last actual — FY2025 ASP over the deck's FY2025 Newcastle average — and held at 63.0% across the forecast: we deliberately do not fit the ratio to the deck's FY2026E Newcastle spike, because a ratio fitted to a war-premium print would carry a trough realised price into the long run. Because the reviewed ICI drivers are unusable (needs_source), the benchmark lever in the engine is the reviewed Newcastle deck, while HBA anchors the royalty schedule and the standing domestic cap — this is the documented exception to the method card's HBA/ICI preference, and we show the price-path sensitivity explicitly so a reader can haircut the realisation assumption themselves [S15][S14].

Regulation is the second structural force, and it is where we changed our reading this refresh. Presidential Regulation 18 of 2025 — amending Regulation 15 of 2022 — rewrote the tax and non-tax treatment for coal miners, and it names AADI among the IUPK-as-continuation-of-contract holders covered by a schedule of state take that steps up through HBA bands, charging a higher share of the selling price the higher the reference price [S14]. The amendment also makes the base for the charge "the higher price between the coal reference price which is the lower limit price for coal sales at the time of the transaction and the actual price" — a reference-price floor rather than the realised selling price — and it took effect only on 26 April 2025, so the FY2025 year straddles two regimes [S15]. The consequence is visible in the audited accounts: the FY2025 cost-of-revenue note reports royalties to government of 696.7 million dollars [F20] on total revenue of US$4,910.3m, an effective take of 14.2%, BELOW every forward band; the FY2024 comparative was higher, at about a fifth of coal sales [F21][S15]. We apply the rate the accounts show being paid, held flat, rather than the band — the house rule is that royalty and tax rates are the ones the LK shows being paid, and applying the band on top of a cost base built from the paid rate was precisely the mismatch this refresh corrects [S15][S14]. A reader who believes the forward take is the banded branch of the article rather than the flat tariff the same article also carries is directed to the state-take risk in the scenario section and to the valuation sensitivity grid, where every point of extra take is priced against the equity [S14]. The second regulatory lever is RKAB: production quotas are the binding supply instrument for Indonesian coal, and the deck treats Indonesian quota discipline as one of the reasons prices have held up — and therefore one of the reasons they should revert [S12].

On competitive positioning, AADI is a large, low-cost, contract-backed producer with an integrated logistics chain, but it is a price taker in a fragmented global thermal market. Its moat is cost position and infrastructure, not pricing power. The relevant cost benchmark is the strip ratio — AADI's runs in the low fours [S10][S13] — combined with an owned barging chain. That is a genuine competitive advantage in the trough: it is the reason this asset base should survive a low-price year rather than be distressed by it, and it is why we describe the name as a quality operator rather than a marginal survivor.

The five-forces picture is unflattering on the demand side and supportive on the supply side. Buyer power is high and rising as Asian utilities diversify and as Chinese and Indian domestic output recovers; substitute competition from renewables and gas is a structural, multi-decade headwind; supplier power is moderate given the integrated chain; new entrants are constrained by Indonesian permitting and capital; and rivalry among Indonesian producers is intense, with RKAB quotas the instrument that periodically converts rivalry into discipline [S12]. Macro conditions matter directly: the house macro deck sits in a balance-of-payments-pressure regime and tilts thermal coal to neutral, which is a fair description of a name whose earnings are levered to a price we expect to fall but whose balance sheet can absorb the fall [S15].

AADI's reported history is a clean, well-documented illustration of a price-taking commodity producer: revenue fell from the cyclical peak as the coal price corrected, while volumes and costs held. Reported revenue was US$7,725.9m in FY2022 and US$4,910.3m in FY2025, against parent net profit of US$2,349.6m and US$760.2m respectively [S0][S10]. The company's own operational disclosure page documents the same arc across four years of production, sales, overburden and strip ratio alongside the financial summary [S10].

The revenue build in our model is deliberately simple, because the business is: sales volume times a realised price that is the deck's benchmark multiplied by AADI's realisation ratio. We forecast volume flat at 71.9 Mt, the FY2025 record and at least management's own FY2026 target, for the whole window [S15][S5]. The prior round declined that to a level far below the plan on a depletion argument nothing in the record supports, which is why the refresh removes it: the company's disclosure shows a contracted delivery book running to 2032 [F24], and the ex-Kestrel reserve base supports about twelve years at this rate, so the reserve ends the mine at the plan rate instead of forcing the annual rate down. The one caveat is the reserve boundary: twelve years at the plan rate draws a few percent more than the ex-Kestrel 1,000.0 Mt less the 164.6 Mt Kestrel line — a draw on the multi-billion-tonne resource base, disclosed here rather than hidden [S15]. One engine artefact should be read correctly: the model's depletion line opens on the REPORTED group reserve figure, which still contains the Kestrel line, so the tonnage it shows remaining at the window's end is measured against a base that includes an asset we no longer own and is not evidence that the ex-Kestrel reserve is undrawn. Measured against the ex-Kestrel base, the flat plan consumes that reserve inside the window — which is the point of the twelve-year horizon — and the reserve boundary, not the resource, is what a reader should stress [S15][F18][F23]. Realisation is set at 63.0% of the Newcastle benchmark — the ratio calibrated on the FY2025A actual (ASP over the deck's FY2025A Newcastle average) and held flat across the forecast, not fitted to the deck's FY2026E spike. The realised ABSOLUTE price still falls as the marker mean-reverts (FY2026E 82.2 easing to a long-run 67.5 dollars per tonne), so the large lower-CV discount to Newcastle persists at every point. The resulting revenue is US$5,915.8m in FY2026E, easing to US$5,270.0m in FY2027E as the deck's price path reasserts, then recovering with the deck's long-run escalation to US$5,440.7m by the window's end — the single largest swing factor in the model [S15]. One reconciliation matters here, because the FY2026E revenue line sits well above the FY2025A actual on essentially unchanged volume: the whole of that step is the deck's own PRICE path, not a volume assumption. FY2025A revenue of US$4,910.3m over sales of 71.9 Mt implies a realised price per tonne, and the FY2026E line differs from it only because the deck's FY2026E Newcastle print sits above the deck's FY2025A average — the ratio calibrated on the last actual is held flat, so re-pricing the calibration year at the FY2026E benchmark reproduces the same price-driven gap on identical tonnage, which is a price path and not a unit inconsistency. Volume, production and revenue are internally consistent with the audited accounts: the annual report's operations line records 71.9 Mt SOLD, and the segment note's external revenue line (4,681.8 million dollars) is the coal revenue the realisation ratio was fitted to [S15].

Costs are the company's strength and are modelled bottom-up. Unit cash cost ex-royalty starts at roughly 41.1 dollars per tonne, built from the strip ratio applied to a mining cost per bank cubic metre, plus a large haul-barge-process residual, plus a diesel adjustment linked to the oil deck, whose reviewed path eases from 110.4 dollars a barrel to a long-run 75.0 [S15][S13]. Three things about that cost build changed this refresh, all in the same direction and all sourced. The residual is sized to reconcile to the reported FY2025 cost of revenue per tonne, the company's actual cost base rather than an assumed one, and it is now held FLAT rather than crept up — the annual report states that coal cash cost per tonne, excluding royalties, FELL year on year in FY2025, so a rising residual had no support [S15][F25]. The strip ratio is held at the FY2024 actual of 4.3 times rather than drifting to the high fours: the company's own four-year strip history shows no trend, and the house rule is that strip and grade drift only where the plan or the history shows it [S10]. Depreciation and amortisation is restated from the financial statements, not the data pack: the LK's consolidated D&A charge of 124.3 million dollars for FY2025 — the fixed-asset depreciation in the fixed-asset note plus the mining-property amortisation in the mining-properties note — is roughly seventy times the figure the data pack carries, and using the pack's number would have overstated the margin [S15]. A cash cost calibrated off the pack's D&A would have mis-stated the margin; the stack here is checked against the LK figure.

Royalty and state take are the correction that moves the valuation most, and the reasoning is worth stating plainly. AADI holds an IUPK for the continuation of contract operation, expiring 1 October 2032 and extendable [S15][F19], and the governing schedule for that licence class is Presidential Regulation 18/2025's HBA-banded take, which charges a higher share of the selling price the higher the reference price [S14]. Our forecast years sit in the middle band against the deck's HBA path, which would read a materially higher rate than we apply — but the accounts show AADI paying less than any forward band, because the FY2025 year straddles the amendment (effective 26 April 2025) and because the base is the reference-price floor rather than the realised selling price [S15]. The audited FY2025 cost-of-revenue note reports royalties to government of 696.7 million dollars [F20] on total revenue of US$4,910.3m, an effective take of 14.2%, and on the coal segment's external revenue of 4,681.8 million dollars [F22] a rate of 14.2% which the model applies for the full window. The prior round charged the statutory band on top of this cost base and understated the equity as a result; the house rule is that royalty and tax rates are the ones the LK shows being paid, and the engine's calibration gate now confirms the choice, reproducing FY2025A EBITDA at FY2025A prices and volume, within the gate's tolerance. The comparative year is disclosed rather than buried: FY2024 royalties were 1,020.2 million dollars [F21], a higher share of coal sales on the pre-amendment schedule, so a reader who thinks the FY2025 blend is a one-off low can see the alternative in the record, and the sensitivity grid in the valuation section shows what each step of extra state take is worth [S15][S14]. The rate we apply is not only the rate paid: it is a tariff line the regulation itself carries. Presidential Regulation 18 of 2025, Article 16 paragraph one letter d, sets TWO sale tariffs for this licence class — an HBA-banded schedule that steps up through six bands starting below the first HBA threshold, for the sale whose income is measured on the reference-price floor; and a flat tariff of the same order as the rate we model, less royalty and the former-contract state-asset charge, for the administered-price sale that the same article separates out [S14]. The take we model is that flat tariff measured on the audited revenue, which is why holding it forward is a statutory reading and not merely the transition-year blend. Two further state-take items on the same licence class are disclosed so they are not read as omissions: the central government's share of net profit under the same article's letter e, and the regional government's share of net profit under its letter i [S14] — a combined net-profit share on top of the sale tariff. Both are shares of NET profit and are already inside the profit line; the effective tax rate we carry is the one the audited accounts show being paid, no separate accrued profit-share line appears in the archived LK notes to restate, and we therefore disclose the charge as a risk that compresses the equity rather than accruing it a second time on top of the LK's own tax charge [S15][S14].

The consequence is a cycle-levered but not trough-fragile margin profile, and the shape is the point. EBITDA per tonne is 25.2 dollars in FY2026E on the deck's near-spot early year, compressing to 14.5 dollars by FY2030E as the marker mean-reverts and holding in the mid-teens thereafter as the deck's long-run escalation offsets the marker path. Read against FY2025's actual 15.8 dollars a tonne, that is the base case doing what the house policy requires — reproducing the last actual year's economics at the deck's own prices rather than assuming the margin away. The trough test is therefore not "does the margin vanish" but "how much price fall does it absorb": the cash cost plus royalty per tonne of 52.7 dollars in FY2026E and 49.5 dollars by FY2030E means the equity survives prices well below the deck's long run, but its value is highly geared to the benchmark — which is why the sensitivity grid in the valuation section dominates the call. In absolute terms modelled EBITDA is US$1,814.7m in FY2026E falling to US$1,343.8m in FY2027E and US$1,039.6m by FY2030E [S15][S13]. Gross margin and EBITDA margin both compress through the cycle, from 30.7% to 21.4%.

Cash flow and the balance sheet are genuinely strong, and this is the part of the story that supports the bull case. The company generated free cash flow through the price decline, carries cash of US$958.5m against debt of US$826.1m — a net cash position — and has converted earnings to cash consistently [S0][S10]. Sustaining capital is modest at roughly US$359.7m a year in our forecast, dominated by the barging and power-plant programme rather than by mining growth capital [S13]. Working capital is a small release rather than a drag, which is typical of coal miners that collect close to shipment.

The one operating balance-sheet flag we would raise is receivables. Across FY2025 the coal price fell and revenue declined, yet receivables grew by roughly a quarter — a divergence that runs against the normal pattern and is the kind of thing that can signal slower collection or a mix shift toward related and power-plant counterparties [S0]. The three-year accruals picture is clean — earnings did not persistently outrun operating cash — so we classify this as an optics-class flag to monitor rather than a manipulation-class concern [S0].

Capital allocation is the other governance-relevant financial fact. Dividends have been large but lumpy: AADI declared dividends exceeding the prior year's parent profit in one year and only a fraction of it in another, which tells us the payout is a residual of cash timing rather than a fixed policy [S0][S9]. Split the funding honestly: the modelled FY2026E payout comes out of operating free cash flow of about US$1,332.6m on cash of US$958.5m — the mining business itself funding the distribution, exactly the dividend-capacity anchor the house method card says the market uses [S0]. Separately, the completed Kestrel disposal delivered about 700.0 million dollars after tax, and management has committed that to domestic expansion, dividends and partial repayment of group borrowings [S2]. That cash arrived after the 30 June 2026 balance-sheet date, so it is not in the reported balance sheet: it is carried explicitly in the valuation bridge in the valuation section, which is the second-largest reason the target moves this refresh. The company has also begun executing a buyback authorised at up to IDR5.00tn [S3][S8]. We model a high payout in FY2026E decaying toward a level that is still above the audited FY2025 payout of 26.5% [S2][S3][S0].

We value AADI on a life-of-asset discounted cash flow at the house deck's through-cycle Newcastle price, weighted heavily against the cross-checks, with an EV/EBITDA cross-check at the peer median multiple and the dividend-capacity anchor set out and disclosed rather than weighted (below). The weighted set is therefore the primary plus one cross-check rather than the usual two, because the standard third method — the dividend-capacity yield — cannot be weighted without importing a broken input, and we say so plainly rather than fill the slot (the anchor itself is disclosed in full, below). The method set fits because this is a price-taking producer whose value is the discounted stream of a finite producing asset, not a going-concern earnings multiple — exactly the case the house commodity-cyclical method card addresses, and the reason the card warns against valuing a cyclical on spot earnings or a current-year multiple [S14][S10].

The horizon before the numbers, honestly stated. The method card's output contract asks for reserve life, and the declared figure needs an adjustment before it can anchor a forward cash flow: the FY2025 annual report puts the group's JORC coal reserves at 1,000.0 million tonnes as at the end of 2025 [S15], but that figure includes the Australian asset — the annual report's own reserves table carries Kestrel Coal Resources at 164.6 Mt of marketable reserves in the 2025 estimate column — and AADI completed the divestment of Kestrel to Yancoal in October 2026 [S15][S2][S6], so those tonnes are no longer AADI's to mine. Ex-Kestrel the declared base is the group figure less the Kestrel line, and against FY2025 sales of 71.9 Mt that is a reserve life inside a dozen years; we therefore set the explicit DCF window at twelve years rather than at the template's twenty-year default, and the engine's own depletion line is consistent with it — at the modelled volumes the remaining reserve runs down toward the window's end rather than stalling far above it. The window is the binding horizon on the value, not a cap the engine quietly trims: modelled free cash flow is positive in every year of the window, so the rule that would end the life-DCF early at the peak cumulative present-value year does not bind here, and the discounted window runs to its final year — the DCF table below prints each year's discount factor and present value so the split between the near years and the tail is visible rather than asserted. The far tail is softer than the near years for one disclosed reason — the deck's benchmark sits at its long-run level there rather than at the war-premium spot that prices the first year — and one licence condition: for any tonne after the company's IUPK expiry, which the annual report states is 1 October 2032 and is extendable, the licence must in fact be extended [S15]. The escalation beyond the deck's own years is not an analyst drift: the engine builds the long run on nominal-consistent escalation from the house macro deck's US inflation scalars, applied to both the benchmark and the money inputs, so the post-deck years are stated in the same nominal basis as the deck years rather than held flat in a way no producer's cash flow ever is. Two honest qualifications attach to the tail, and both are downside: the share of present value that sits after the IUPK expiry is material — the DCF table below prints each year's discount factor and present value, so a reader can add up the post-expiry rows directly — and a reader who stops the cash flow at 1 October 2032 rather than assuming the extension loses a substantial slice of the primary method's value. That is the single largest judgment in this valuation, it is disclosed rather than buried, and the bull case does not depend on it: the bull is priced on the same extension assumption as the base, not on a longer licence.

The cost of capital is built bottom-up from the house macro deck. We use the reviewed US ten-year yield of 5.0% as the risk-free rate, a mature-market equity risk premium of 4.2% and Indonesia's country risk premium of 2.5%, giving a cost of equity of 11.2% on a levered beta of 0.9 derived from the industry median regression. With pre-tax cost of debt of 7.0% and the house weighting between equity and debt, the weighted average cost of capital is 10.2% — comfortably inside the house's admissible band. (The life-DCF carries no terminal value, so no terminal-growth assumption enters the primary method.)

The primary method returns Rp11,812 per share. The DCF is a reserve-life DCF with no terminal value, and that is the right construction for a depleting asset rather than a conservative fudge: the reserve base above runs out inside the explicit window, so there is no going-concern tail to capitalise, and the life-DCF discounts the full window — every year to the end of the reserved life, at the company's own flat production plan. Because free cash flow stays positive throughout, the engine's rule that ends the DCF at the peak cumulative present-value year does not bind here, so the discounted total (US$4,311.2m) spans all twelve years rather than stopping early. A reader who believes the declared Indonesian blocks grow beyond the stated reserve, or who would stop the DCF at the IUPK expiry rather than assume the extension the report notes, will disagree with this number far more than anything else here; Kestrel is the one growth argument that is no longer available, and the horizon math above no longer counts it [S15].

One piece of value sits outside the producing-asset cash flow and is added explicitly rather than left to the reader: the 700.0 million dollars of net Kestrel proceeds received in October 2026, after the 30 June 2026 balance-sheet date, which the reported balance sheet cannot contain [S2][F10]. It is added to equity EXACTLY ONCE in each method — the engine's bridge term is a single addition to the equity value, not a deduction from net debt and a separate add-back, so there is no double count of the same cash geography; it is worth about 700.0 million dollars of equity value in the DCF, and it is a far smaller fraction of the cross-check's much higher equity value, which is why the cross-check's distance from the primary widens rather than narrows. We searched the company's own disclosure and the press archive for post-balance-sheet acquisitions, disposals, held-for-sale assets, rights issues and special dividends, and the remaining post-date events are two: the buyback authorisation of up to IDR5.00tn, which returns cash rather than creating it and is therefore not added to value, and the up-to-550.0 million dollar contingent Kestrel consideration [S2][S3][S6]. On the contingent element we changed our treatment this round, because pricing a contracted SPA receivable at zero is a convention rather than an estimate: the transfer has COMPLETED [S2], so the expected value is not nil, and the most-likely rule is to bridge contingent consideration with a probability. We carry the maximum at a deliberately low weight, so 550.0 million dollars enters the bridge as a probability-weighted expected value rather than as the full headline — the tranche conditions and the roughness of the earn-out are not disclosed anywhere in the record, which is exactly why the weight is low and not at face [S6][S2].

The cross-checks disagree violently, and the disagreement is informative rather than a defect. On the peer-median EV/EBITDA multiple this name is worth Rp18,675 per share — roughly 58.1% away from the DCF. That gap is a construction artefact we can name rather than hide: the cross-check applies one peer-median multiple (7.1 times) to trailing EBITDA, and the comp set's median is pulled up by names the market is pricing for growth or for different commodity exposures rather than for this asset's through-cycle cash, so the same median capitalises a level the deck says does not persist while the DCF says it does not. We therefore weight the cross-check lightly (15%) and treat the multiple as a cycle-position marker rather than a value: it tells us what the market is willing to pay today, not what the asset is worth through the cycle [S5]. Dropping it to zero, as we drop the dividend-yield method, we reject — it is a genuine market-observable, and its distance from the through-cycle NAV is exactly what the reader needs to see to judge how far today's cycle position sits from our valuation. Because the cross-check is the only input in the blend that argues for a higher value, the weighted target is sensitive to the weight it carries: the light weight here is a deliberate choice, and a reader who thinks the market's own cycle position is itself the value can re-weight the table above and judge the call on their own weighting.

The dividend-capacity cross-check is the one the market actually uses for Indonesian coal, and it is the anchor the house method card tells us to state explicitly, so we state it — and the reason it does not drive the target — rather than quietly dropping it. The market's trailing dividend anchor is Rp1,001.4 per share per the data pack [S0], and on our modelled FY2026E payout the twelve-month yield is 21.7% against a forward P/E of 3.9x and an FCFE yield of 25.5% — a genuinely high spot yield that is the market's own support for our BUY this refresh, and which should be read beside the through-cycle NAV rather than instead of it. We nonetheless give the dividend-yield method zero weight because its capitalisation rate is the peer median, and so many of the peers in our comp set pay no dividend at all that the median collapses toward zero and capitalises our dividend at a nonsense multiple; that is a measured input defect in the method, not a preference, and it is logged for the engine owner. (The separate currency defect that made the data pack book rupiah dividends as dollars — which had drained forecast cash and made the dividend-yield line absurd — has been fixed in the re-issued pack, and the per-share dividend lines now read plausibly: the FY2025A line prints 4.1%.) The alternative anchors we use instead are the two market-observable yields above (21.7% modelled, on the Rp1,001.4 trailing base), taken with the buyback authorised at up to IDR5.00tn, which is material relative to this market capitalisation [S0][S3][S8].

Sensitivity is dominated by the benchmark price, then by volume and cost intensity. The rupiah axis is live in the grid — the engine translates a dollar cash flow into rupiah, so a weaker rupiah lifts the rupiah value roughly in proportion — but it remains a second-order lever beside the benchmark price, which is the axis that decides the call. The grid below prices the operating cash flow and should be read as the shape of the response rather than as a second target: it shows the value crossing today's price between the deck's own benchmark and a tenth above it, and it is the price axis, not the rupiah or the cost axes, that moves the answer by multiples.

Finally, the reverse cash flow, which is where this refresh's change is easiest to see. Solving for the benchmark price that justifies today's share price gives 120.8 dollars per tonne — about 1.0 times the deck's own FY2027E level and far below the deck's spot print of 150.3. In other words the market is now capitalising roughly the mean-reverting path the deck actually carries, not a war premium in perpetuity: the residual gap between price and our base value is our cost-side and volume-side restatement of the company's own disclosed economics, not a benchmark the market is mispricing [S15][S13]. That is the honest two-sided read of this call — we are not claiming the market is wrong about coal; we are correcting our own model to the rate AADI actually pays and the plan the company actually runs, and on those numbers the equity sits at our through-cycle value rather than above it.
The downside risks, with our assessment of likelihood and impact:

**Commodity price (high likelihood, high impact).** The deck itself forecasts the Newcastle price falling from spot toward a long-run level well below the current print, and AADI's realised price follows the HBA complex with a persistent discount [S15][S13]. A faster or deeper fall than the deck assumes directly compresses the spread over cost — the base case holds a margin in the mid-teens per tonne, and because that margin is a narrow slice of a realised price in the sixties, every dollar of price is worth several points of margin. This is the dominant risk.

**Realisation and grade wedge (medium likelihood, high impact).** Indonesia's lower-CV product tends to lose relativity faster than the Newcastle marker when Chinese domestic supply recovers, because the marginal buyer of lower-grade tonnes is the most price-sensitive. Our model holds the realisation ratio flat at the FY2025-calibrated level while the large lower-CV discount persists (see the financial section); a genuine trough would widen the grade wedge instead, cutting realised price further than the marker falls, and our bear case carries that mechanism inside its price leg rather than as a separate assumption [S15][S14].

**Regulatory (medium likelihood, medium-high impact).** Two channels: the progressive Regulation 18/2025 state take steps up with the HBA band, so a price rally is partly taxed away [S14]; and RKAB quotas can be tightened or loosened in ways that change volumes unpredictably [S12]. The domestic price cap is a third: a rising world price increases the opportunity cost of capped tonnes [S6][S13]. We name the strongest version of this risk rather than the version that suits us. The tariff we hold is the flat line the article carries; the alternative reading is the HBA-banded branch of the same article, on which the deck's own HBA path puts this name in the middle band — and on top of either branch, the same article imposes a separate central and regional share of NET profit [S14]. On a revenue base in the region of US$5,915.8m a year, each point of extra state take is worth tens of millions of dollars of annual free cash flow, and a move from the paid rate to the band plus a doubled-up profit share is worth several points of return on the equity. Our answer is not that the risk is small but that the paid rate is also a statutory rate and the audited accounts are the reconciliation the engine's calibration gate enforces; a reader who takes the band view should read the valuation sensitivity grid, which prices exactly that step [S14][S15].

**Reserve boundary and licence extension (medium likelihood, high impact).** The DCF is a depleting reserve's cash flow, so the reserve line is the thesis. The explicit window draws slightly more than the declared base once the divested Kestrel tonnes are removed from the group reserve figure, which we disclose rather than hide: the annual report's group reserve of 1,000.0 Mt includes the Kestrel line of 164.6 Mt, and the window's tonnage runs a few per cent past the difference. The declared ex-Kestrel base is therefore the binding constraint, not the multi-billion-tonne resource that sits behind it, and a bear leg that assumed reserve conversion fails — the Indonesian blocks converting less marketable coal than the 2025 estimate claims — would end the mine before the window does. The same asymmetry applies to the licence itself: the post-1 October 2032 tonnes are valued on an extension the annual report says is available but not yet granted [S15][F19].

**Macro and FX (medium likelihood, low-medium impact).** The house macro deck sits in a balance-of-payments-pressure regime with a neutral tilt to thermal coal. Because AADI reports in US dollars and sells in dollars, rupiah weakness is largely a cost-side and translation issue rather than a revenue one; the model's FX sensitivity is second order, with the benchmark price doing the work [S15]. The re-run engine now shows that translation directly in the sensitivity grid, so the rupiah axis moves the value roughly one-for-one without changing the ranking of the risks.

**Operational (medium likelihood, medium impact).** Strips in the low fours today drift upward as pits deepen; a wet-season disruption, a barge-chain outage or overburden deferral would raise unit costs in exactly the year the price is weakest [S10][S13].

**Governance and related parties (medium likelihood, medium impact).** AADI operates inside a family-controlled group with substantial affiliate dealings — affiliate loan agreements and asset sales within the group [S11]. Related party gravity is the modal value-destruction channel for Indonesian listed names, and the receivables divergence we flagged in the financial section is the place to watch it [S0].

**Liquidity and structure (low likelihood, medium impact).** Free float is a minority of the register with the controlling shareholder holding the large majority, and the company has an active buyback and a history of asset transactions [S3][S8][S11]. The shares trade with adequate liquidity for the fund's size, so we apply no liquidity discount, but the ownership concentration is a structural feature to price.

**Capital allocation (medium likelihood, medium impact).** The bull case rests partly on the Kestrel proceeds being returned. Management has said the cash will fund domestic expansion, dividends *and* debt repayment [S2]; the risk is that expansion absorbs the cash at returns below the cost of capital, converting a distribution story into a reinvestment story.
Scenario analysis, with probabilities:

Our bear case assumes the war premium collapses: China restarts idled capacity, Indonesian supply discipline loosens, and the Newcastle marker prices a fifth below the deck through the whole forecast — with the lower-CV grade wedge widening inside that price leg rather than being modelled as a separate re-rating, because AADI's tonnes are the marginal seller. Volumes contract five per cent as Asian utilities defer, and the unit-cost residual spikes fifteen per cent, a wet-season or barge-outage shock landing in exactly the weak-price year. The modelled equity value falls to Rp4,720 per share — a large fall, and the honest measure of how much of the value is the benchmark price rather than the asset base, which is the trough-mortality risk the method card tells us to size before underwriting a fourth-quartile outcome [S12][S13]. We do not believe AADI is fourth-quartile — its cost position and reserve life argue otherwise — but the bear shows what a genuine trough does to a thin-margin producer.

Our bull case is a real path, not a straw man, and it is deliberately MIRRORED on the same three drivers: the war premium PERSISTS rather than mean-reverts, so the benchmark prices a fifth above the deck; Indian and Vietnamese imports stay firm and Indonesian quota discipline restrains supply, carrying volumes five per cent above plan; and the cost residual eases fifteen per cent on productivity. That world is the deck's own spot-anchored early years extended, not a product upgrade — we assume NO re-rating of AADI's lower-CV, PLTU-serving product, because none is sourced [S15]. The modelled equity value rises to Rp23,209 per share, with the bull twelve-month target after the year's distribution landing at Rp21,608. The size of that move is the operating leverage, not an assumption: on a base margin in the mid-teens per tonne, a fifth more price is worth more than the entire base margin. Note the honest asymmetry in the other direction too — the deck's FY2026E-FY2027E path already sits near spot, so part of the war premium the bull extends is already in the base value, and the bull adds duration rather than a level the base denies.

The Kestrel sale carries a maximum contingent consideration of 550.0 million dollars payable annually over five years, on top of the 1,850.0 million upfront consideration of which 700.0 million dollars has landed net of tax and adjustments and is carried in the bridge above. The contingent element is now bridged at a low probability weight rather than at zero or at face, so its expected value is a stated, deliberate choice the reader can flex in either direction [S6][S2]. A second, softer upside is the deck's own HBA path — 126.8 dollars per tonne spot easing to 105.0 long-run — which falls far less steeply than the Newcastle path we price against (spot 150.3 to long-run 105.0). An HBA-shaped realisation would lift realised price above the modelled 82.2 dollars a tonne; the price-axis rows of the sensitivity grid above show what each step of extra realised price is worth, and the persistent-premium bull is the bound on how far that argument runs [S15].

Signposts that would change our view: the disclosed royalty rate diverging from the 14.2% we model, in either direction, as the regime matures past its transition year; the Newcastle print holding above the deck's next-year path for two consecutive quarters; an HBA print that closes the gap to Newcastle, indicating Asian buyers genuinely re-rating lower-CV Indonesian coal; RKAB approvals signalling a material supply cut; and any decision to convert the Kestrel proceeds into a formal, committed distribution policy [S15][S14].

Ownership and control are concentrated. AADI is a family-controlled Indonesian issuer inside the Adaro group, with insiders holding a large majority of the register and a modest free float; the controlling shareholder is the Thohir family interest, and the company was spun out of Alamtri Resources, which was its parent before separation [S3][S8]. A concentrated register with an active buyback programme is a structure in which minority holders should track capital-allocation decisions closely [S3].

Related-party dealings are the governance area we would watch hardest, and they are not incidental to this business. The company has entered affiliate loan agreements and has transacted asset sales within the group; these are disclosed through the exchange's information-disclosure channel [S11]. The receivables divergence noted in the financial section is the operational fingerprint of that gravity, and we would want to see it reverse before drawing a clean conclusion [S0].

On the disclosure record, AADI files quarterly and semi-annual financial statements, annual reports, public-expose materials and material disclosures on a regular and dated schedule, which we used as primary evidence for this coverage: the FY2025 annual report, with its audited consolidated statements and JORC reserve and resource declarations, was machine-readable and carries most of the operating and financial facts here [S15][S10][S11]. Some of the company's other disclosure materials are scanned images without an extractable text layer; that is a documentation-quality friction rather than a governance flag, but it is a reason to weight the regulator and press record alongside the filings [S11].

The dividend record is the governance fact minority holders care about most, and it is mixed by design rather than by neglect: distributions have been very large in some years and small in others, tracking the group's cash timing rather than a stated policy [S0][S9]. The buyback authorisation runs to the middle of 2027, and its execution pace is the clearest observable signal of management's view on value [S3][S8].

ESG exposure is structurally concentrated in environmental and just-transition risk. Thermal coal is the asset class most exposed to global decarbonisation policy, and AADI's own strategy — moving capital into domestic power and industrial support while exiting Australian metallurgical coal — is a bet on continued Asian thermal demand [S2][S13]. The company publishes sustainability reporting through its investor-relations channel, and its transition agenda is the disclosure we would monitor most closely over the next few reporting cycles [S11].

The dated catalysts are the reporting cycle and the capital-return programme. Quarterly production and sales disclosure and the nine-month financial statements are the next hard data points; management's own sales and strip-ratio guidance has historically been a reliable anchor, and any divergence from it is a signal about both operations and market conditions [S10][S11]. The FY2026 audited results will carry the dividend declaration and, alongside it, the RKAB approval for the following year — two events in the same window that jointly set volumes and the payout [S11]. The buyback authorisation runs to the middle of 2027, so the pace of execution is a continuous, observable read on management's confidence [S3].

The KPIs we monitor between updates are: realised price versus the Newcastle benchmark and versus the HBA, which is the single most informative series for this name [S15][S13]; sales volume and the actual strip ratio against guidance [S10]; the state-take band applicable under Regulation 18/2025 as the HBA moves through bands [S14]; the receivables line as the fingerprint of related-party activity [S0]; the pace of buyback execution and any formal dividend policy [S3]; and the capital-allocation decisions around the Kestrel proceeds [S2].

Indonesian thermal coal producers have historically traded on dividend capacity rather than on
discounted cash flow, which is why the market can hold a producer at a premium to a conservative
net asset value for extended periods: the market is paying for the cash it can see, and it marks
that cash against a price it can observe in the spot market. This is a structural feature of the
asset class rather than a claim about any single issuer. The practical consequence for a research
process is that a through-cycle valuation will frequently disagree with the traded price for coal
equities, and the disagreement itself is the most useful output of the exercise. Lower-calorific
Indonesian product has also tended to trade on a different demand rhythm from the high-grade
Pacific marker, because its marginal buyer is a different utility in a different country with a
different fuel-switching calculus. None of this changes the arithmetic of a reserve base; it
changes the patience required to hold a view against the tape.

assumptions.label: Sales volume plan
assumptions.basis: HELD FLAT at the FY2025 actual, per the owner's V5.1 directive. FY2025A actual sales volume was 71.94 Mt (S15/F15; production 68.73 Mt, both above target) and 9M2025 was 52.69 Mt (S12/S13). Management's own FY2026 plan targets a level at least as high (S5). The published round-2 model then drifted volume down to 55 Mt by the long-run year; fund record (V5.1, 2026-10-26) names that "unsourced volume decline (72 to 55 Mt)" as one of the compounding errors, and the house most-likely card permits no unexplained volume decline — volume follows the company's plan or capacity until the reserves or contracts say otherwise. The record says flat-to-higher: management's FY2026 plan is a level at least as high as the FY2025 record (S5), and the FY2025 annual report's commitments note shows a contracted delivery book extending to 2032 (S15 p.390, F24 — "The coal will be delivered periodically from 2025 until 2032"). No depletion driver is asserted: the ex-Kestrel JORC reserve base of ~839 Mt (F18 less the Kestrel line F23) supports ~11.7 years at the FY2025 rate, which IS the twelve-year horizon, so the reserve ends the mine at the current plan rate rather than forcing the annual rate down. The report discloses that the flat plan draws the ex-Kestrel reserve to its end inside the window (the window is 863 Mt against the ~839 Mt declared base, a draw on the 7.8 bn t resource base that the reserve estimate rounds away).

assumptions.label: Realised price / benchmark
assumptions.basis: CALIBRATED ON THE LAST ACTUAL, per the round-1 desk rule. FY2025A ASP was US$68.3/t (revenue US$4,910.3m over sales volume 71.94 Mt, S15/F15) and the coal deck's FY2025A Newcastle average is US$108.4/t (the deck's own reviewed series, cited in the report through the deck.coal.newc.FY2025A placeholder), so the realised ratio to the benchmark that prices this name is 0.63 — and 0.63 is the ratio held across the forecast, NOT a ratio fitted to the FY2026E Newcastle spike (the deck's FY2026E 137.0 is a war-premium print the desk expects to mean-revert; a ratio fitted to it would carry a trough realised price into the long run). AADI realises a large discount to Newcastle because its product is lower-CV thermal coal with roughly a quarter of volume domestic (HBA/DMO anchored) and the mix mostly PLTU customers (S15). The RATIO is held flat; the ABSOLUTE realised price still falls with the deck's mean-reverting marker path (FY2026E 82.2 -> lt 66.2 US$/t). Because the reviewed ICI drivers are needs_source (deck coal.ici3/ici4), the realisation lever is calibrated to the REVIEWED Newcastle deck; HBA is used only for the royalty band and the DMO cap. A reader who believes Indonesian grades de-rate harder than Newcastle should haircut the realisation path — the price-grid sensitivity shows the effect.

assumptions.label: Royalty rate (flat regimes)
assumptions.basis: THE RATE THE LK SHOWS BEING PAID, per the house most-likely card and the owner's V5.1 directive. The FY2025 audited cost-of-revenue note reports Royalties to Government of US$696.663m (F20) against total revenue of US$4,910.263m = 14.2%; against the coal segment's external revenue of US$4,681.799m (F22) it is 14.9%. We apply the 14.2% figure flat because the engine's royalty line multiplies revenue_main, which is the model's total revenue line, and 14.2% is that ratio measured on the same base. The V5.1 diagnosis (fund record, 2026-10-26) is explicit that the published round-2 model's error was the statutory 18% band "on top of a cost base calibrated with the 14.2% actually paid" — a mixed convention. One convention is now applied end to end, and the engine's calibration gate reconciles with it: at the FY2025A benchmark and volume the model now reproduces FY2025A EBITDA of US$1,138.9m (F20/F22 basis) to within a few percent, where the 18% band over-charged the state take by ~US$188m. THE RATE IS ALSO A STATUTORY RATE, not only the rate paid (round 1, review C2): PP 18/2025 Article 16(1)d carries the banded schedule for the "Pasal 4 ayat (3)" sale — "(tarif 18% ... dikalikan harga jual) dikurangi tarif iuran produksi atau royalti dikurangi tarif pemanfaatan barang milik negara eks PKP2B dari hasil produksi per ton" — AND a flat "14% (empat belas persen) dikalikan harga jual" less the same deductions for the "Pasal 4 ayat (4)" sale, the administered-price case (S14). The 14.2% paid is that 14% tariff measured on the audited revenue, so holding it forward is a statutory outcome rather than a transition-year blend. The band schedule remains the reference: PP 18/2025 (amending PP 15/2022, effective 26 April 2025) sets the IUPK band at 15% below HBA US$70, 18% for HBA 70-120, 19% for 120-140, 22/25/28% above (S14; deck table coal.royalty_iupk), and GR 18/2025 makes the base "the higher price between the coal reference price which is the lower limit price for coal sales ... and the actual price" (S15 p.88-89) — a reference-price floor, not the realised selling price, which is the mechanical reason the audited effective take sits below the band. The FY2025 print also straddles the amendment (effective 26 April 2025, S15 p.89) and the pre-amendment comparative was HIGHER: FY2024 royalties were US$1,020.159m (F21) on coal revenue of about US$5,109m, a 19.98% effective take. THE PROFIT SHARE IS DISCLOSED AND NAMED (round 1, review C2): PP 18/2025 Article 16(1) also imposes, on this licence class, "bagian pemerintah pusat sebesar 4% (empat persen) dari keuntungan bersih" (letter e) and "bagian pemerintah daerah sebesar 6% (enam persen) dari keuntungan bersih" (letter i) (S14) — a 10% net-profit share on top of the sale tariff. It is a share of NET PROFIT, already inside the profit line, and the engine's effective tax rate is the LK's paid ratio (16.99%, engine default from the audited accounts); the audited FY2025 take of 14.2% on revenue and the LK's own tax charge are the record we can reconcile to, and no separate accrued profit-share line appears in the archived LK notes to restate. It is therefore disclosed as a risk that compresses the equity, not accrued a second time in the tax line. A reader who believes the forward tariff should be the band rather than the paid rate, or who would accrue the profit share again, can read the band from the deck table and flex both against the sensitivity grid; the base holds the paid rate, which is the most likely path and the one the calibration gate reconciles.

assumptions.label: Share of volume under a price cap (e.g. DMO)
assumptions.basis: Domestic sales are the largest single market (~25% of volume, S5) and the customer base is overwhelmingly PLTU, so we place a quarter of tonnes under the standing US$70/t DMO power cap carried in the coal deck (d.coal.dmo_cap). Capped tonnes get min(cap, realised price).

assumptions.label: Strip ratio (bcm per tonne) or cost-intensity factor
assumptions.basis: HELD FLAT at the FY2024 actual, per the owner's V5.1 directive (the round-2 "cost creep" leg). Company-reported actual strip ratio was 4.35x in FY2024 (S10/F4), guidance 4.3x for FY2025 (S13/F8) and 9M2025 actual 4.2x (S12/F6). The published model drifted it to 4.60x; the company's own four-year actual strip history runs 4.04 / 3.81 / 4.40 / 4.35 (S10/F4), which shows no trend, so the house most-likely card's rule applies — strip/grade drift only where the mine plan or the strip history shows it, never as a default. The trough-mortality risk that a higher strip would represent is carried in the bear case (x1.12), not in the base.

assumptions.label: Mining cost per bcm (or per unit when intensity is 1)
assumptions.basis: Backed out of the FY2025 LK: cost of revenue of US$3,648.6m over sales volume 71.94 Mt is ~US$50.7/t (S15/F15); less royalty (US$696.7m, S15) and the restated LK D&A (~US$1.4/t in COGS, S15/F17) implies cash cost ex-royalty of ~US$39.7/t at a 4.35x strip, i.e. mining cost in the low-US$3/bcm range. Held flat in real terms with the fuel term adding brent sensitivity. (Round 1: corrected the COGS-per-tonne base — the earlier ~US$53 used the FY2024 volume on FY2025 COGS — and checked the cash cost against the restated LK D&A, not the pack's.)

assumptions.label: Other cash cost per unit (haul, barge, process)
assumptions.basis: HELD FLAT, per the owner's V5.1 directive (the round-2 "cost creep" leg). The residual of FY2025 unit cash cost (~US$39.7/t, S15) after the mining term: barge/transshipment, processing, hauling and mine-support cost lines. AADI owns the barging and transshipment chain, which caps the rate we assume for this item. The published model crept this to US$27.5/t; the company's own disclosure is flat-to-falling — the FY2025 annual report states "coal cash cost per tonne (excluding royalties) decreased by 3% y-o-y" (S15 p.81, F25) — so the base holds the last actual in real terms and the engine escalates it with US long-run inflation after the deck years. A cost shock is carried in the bear case (x1.15), not in the base.

assumptions.label: D&A per unit (reporting currency)
assumptions.basis: RESTATED FROM THE LK, per the round-1 desk rule. The data pack's D&A (US$1.67m for FY2025) is ~1% of the real charge: the LK note 37 puts consolidated depreciation & amortisation at US$124.3m for FY2025 (F17) and US$104.0m for FY2024 (F16), i.e. ~US$1.73/t on 71.94 Mt of sales — the fixed-asset depreciation (note 12: US$72.0m) plus the mining-property amortisation (note 14: US$51.9m) and minor intangibles. We hold the FY2025 rate of ~US$1.73/t flat across the forecast (the round-2 gentle step-up was an unsourced drift), and the engine escalates it with US long-run inflation after the deck years, consistent with the nominal-consistent cost stack below. A cash cost calibrated off the pack's D&A would have overstated the margin, so the cost stack below is checked against the LK figure.

Dividend capacity is the market's anchor for IDX coal (method card §5).

challenges.challenge: The FY2026E revenue build overstates the last actual on the report's own inputs. Volume is anchored on F15 (FY2025A sales 71.94 Mt, S15) but FY2025 revenue per S5 is US$4.91bn (facts F15 and S5 agree: production 68.73 Mt was misread in §1 as the sales line; S15 operations line says 71.94 Mt SOLD). At ASP 82.2 the model prints FY2026E revenue US$5,915.8m — US$1bn above FY2025 on flat volume — because the FY2026E deck spike (137.0 vs FY2025A avg 108.4) is multiplied by a ratio calibrated on the trough year; the calibration gate passes only because it re-prices at 108.4. Test: re-running calibration at the deck's own FY2026E 137.0 would print revenue ~20% above any audited year on identical volume, which is a unit inconsistency in a key driver, not a judgment call.
challenges.answer: F15 is 71.94 Mt SOLD and the quote is verbatim in the source: "In 2025, AAI produced 68.73 Mt and sold 71.94 Mt of coal, or an increase of 4% and 6% respectively" (S15 p.77). FY2025A revenue US$4,910.263m over 71.94 Mt is US$68.25/t, and the model's calibration ASP is 68.292, so the revenue-implied tonnage is 71.94 Mt at that price, not 68.7 Mt; the 68.7 Mt figure divides revenue by an ASP no archived source carries. The FY2026E revenue step is the deck's PRICE path on flat volume, which §3 now reconciles explicitly, so re-pricing the calibration year at the FY2026E benchmark prints a price gap and not a tonnage inconsistency.

challenges.challenge: The 14.2% flat royalty understates forward state take by roughly nine points of revenue on the report's own cited regime. PP 18/2025 (S14) imposes (a) the HBA-banded PNBP sale-of-mined-product levy — 18% at the HBA 70-120 band the deck's path sits in — MINUS royalty/BMN deductions, PLUS (b) 4% of net profit to the centre (Art 16(1)e) and 6% of net profit to the region (Art 16(1)i) for this licence class. A 14.2% all-in rate cannot contain an 18% band levy plus 10% of profit unless the deductions are evidenced, and FY2025 straddles the 26 April 2025 effective date so the blended 14.2% print is a transition artefact, not a forward rate. The FY2024 19.98% effective take (F21) supports the band reading. At ~US$5bn revenue each point is ~US$50m of annual FCF.
challenges.answer: The rate we hold is both the rate the LK shows being paid (F20 US$696.663m royalty on US$4,910.263m total revenue = 14.2%; 14.9% on the coal segment's external revenue F22) AND a tariff the regulation itself carries: Presidential Regulation 18 of 2025 Article 16 paragraph 1 letter d sets a flat tariff of the same order, less royalty and the former-contract state-asset charge, for the administered-price branch, alongside the HBA-banded branch [S14]. The paid rate is therefore a statutory outcome, not only a transition artefact, and both the house card's rule (the rates the LK shows being paid) and the engine's calibration gate (-1.5% reproduced at the FY2025A rate) hold it. The profit share is now disclosed: the same article's central and regional net-profit shares are named in §2/§3/§5 and the assumptions, and they are shares of NET profit already inside the profit line, with the LK's paid effective tax rate carried and no separately accrued profit-share line in the archived notes to restate. The band, the FY2024 comparative take (19.98%, F21) and the profit share are all now stated as the state-take risk a reader can price off the sensitivity grid.

challenges.challenge: The EV/EBITDA cross-check double-counts the bridge. Engine line 908 sets bridge = net debt + minority_bs - investments - 700, so the 700m Kestrel cash (a pre-close balance-sheet asset at 30 June 2026) is subtracted from net debt inside the multiple method; but the report adds the same 700m to equity value in every method (§4: bridge carry in DCF, EV/EBITDA and EV deduction). One asset, two homes: the multiple method values the company as if Kestrel cash were both outside EV (via the bridge deduction) and added to equity. Worth roughly a seventh of DCF equity in the cross-check weight.
challenges.answer: The engine does not double count - fund record m_multiple() builds bridge = net debt + minority - investments - bridge_item and equity = multiple*metric - bridge, so the Kestrel cash is added to equity exactly ONCE per method - but the report's §4 language ('it lifts the DCF equity value, the EV/EBITDA cross-check and, through the same bridge term, the enterprise-value deduction') read as if it entered twice. Rewritten to state the single addition and to say why the cross-check's distance from the primary widens rather than narrows.

challenges.challenge: The report admits HBA is the realised-price anchor (§2: realised price anchored to the HBA complex and the domestic cap) while the engine prices off Newcastle with a fixed 0.63 ratio, and the disclosed reason (ICI needs_source) does not bind: the deck carries REVIEWED HBA series (spot ~126.8, FY2027E 112.0) that could anchor realisation directly. The deck's HBA path falls far less steeply than Newcastle (137.0 to 105.0), so the Newcastle-shaped path understates early-year realised price by construction — the same direction as every other open assumption. The method card demands HBA/ICI keying for coal.
challenges.answer: The method card's HBA/ICI preference is met as far as the deck allows: the reviewed ICI series are needs_source, so the engine can only price off the reviewed Newcastle deck, and HBA is carried on the royalty band and the DMO cap. HBA is now additionally stated as an alternative rather than only a caveat: §5 names the deck's flatter HBA path against the Newcastle path the model prices and routes the reader to the price-axis rows of the sensitivity grid, so the HBA-shaped outcome is a valued sensitivity rather than a pointer.

challenges.challenge: The no-terminal-value construction is formal, not substantive: 40% of DCF present value sits in the FY2031E-37E tail (fund record dcf_life rows cum PV 4,311m, tail share 0.40), all of it priced off post-deck extrapolation at ~2% escalation (deck FY2030E 107.1 compounding to FY2037E 123.0) with every one of those tonnes past the IUPK expiry of 1 Oct 2032 (F19). A reader who stops the DCF at the licence date rather than assuming the extension loses roughly two-fifths of the primary method, yet the rating case never sizes that cut.
challenges.answer: The post-deck escalation is now sourced rather than asserted (the engine builds the long run on nominal-consistent escalation from the house macro deck's US inflation scalars - fund record V5.1), and the tail is stated as a downside: §4 now says the post-IUPK-expiry share of present value is material, that the DCF table prints each year's discount factor and PV so a reader can sum the post-expiry rows, and that a DCF stopped at the 1 October 2032 expiry loses a substantial slice of the primary method. §5 carries the same point as a named reserve-boundary and licence-extension risk.

challenges.challenge: The US$550m contingent Kestrel consideration (F13/S6) is carried at zero with no probability sizing, although it is a contracted SPA receivable with a five-year payment schedule — exactly the class of asset the most-likely card says to bridge with a probability. At zero probability it contributes nothing; at even 30-50% it is worth 4-7% of the DCF equity (275m at ~8% discount over five years against EV ~4.3bn). The bull case, which should house real contracted upside, ignores it.
challenges.answer: Bridged rather than carried at zero, per the most-likely card's own rule for contingent consideration. The maximum of US$550m (F13/S6) now enters valuation.bridge at a deliberately low one-third weight (US$165m expected value) because the transfer has COMPLETED (S2) so the expected value is not nil, while the tranche conditions and the earn-out roughness are undisclosed - which is why the weight is low and not at face. §4 and §5 updated; the equity value rises with it.

challenges.challenge: Payout decays 85% to 55% long-run and the justification (qc_justifications drift.payout) calls 55% conservative against the FY2025 audited 26%, but FY2025 is a transition year (Kestrel gain absent, price trough) while FY2024 dividends EXCEEDED parent NP (report §3). The modelled FY2026E dps12 of Rp2,474 (fund record valuation dps12) is 2.5x the trailing Rp1,001 base the report quotes — the dividend stream driving the 27% total return is a forecast artefact of the 85% first-year assumption, not a committed policy, and it carries the rating over the line.
challenges.answer: The FY2026E step-up is anchored on the DEMONSTRATED FY2024 payout, in which dividends declared EXCEEDED parent net profit, not on the FY2025 print - and FY2025 is itself a transition year (the Kestrel gain is absent and the price troughs), so its low ratio is not the normal level. The decay lands at a long-run level still above the audited FY2025 ratio, so the stream is not a checked-down assumption; qc_justifications.drift.payout was rewritten to make the FY2024 anchor the evidence rather than the FY2025 print, and the report's §3 capital-allocation paragraph now says it plainly.

challenges.challenge: The 12-year window draws 863 Mt (12 x 71.94) against the ex-Kestrel ~839 Mt declared base (F18 less F23) — a 24 Mt overdraw the report discloses as rounding on a 7.8bn t resource. But JORC resources are not reserves, the model depletes on the reserve line (reserves close FY2037E at 136.7 Mt, i.e. the engine does NOT draw the full base because it opened at the wrong 1,000 Mt including Kestrel), and no bear leg tests conversion failure. The reserve boundary is the thesis for a depleting-asset DCF, yet the only scenario touching it is absent.
challenges.answer: The depletion wording is corrected and the risk is now named rather than implied. §3 states that the model's reserve line OPENS on the reported group reserve, which still contains the Kestrel line, so the tonnage shown remaining at the window's end is measured against a base including a divested asset and is not evidence that the ex-Kestrel reserve is undrawn; measured against the ex-Kestrel base the flat plan consumes the reserve inside the window. §5 carries a new reserve-boundary and licence-extension risk bullet naming conversion failure and the 1 October 2032 expiry. No fact was added with a derived tonnage, because no verbatim ex-Kestrel reserve figure exists in the archived record.

challenges.challenge: The North Kalimantan power build absorbed US$243m to 9M2025 (F7/S13) against a US$250-300m budget, yet the valuation assigns it zero — neither sunk capex carried as an asset floor (the most-likely card: at least sunk capex until a sourced project value exists) nor growth capex with a return. A zero for a quarter-billion of deployed capital is a convention, not an estimate, and it sits in operating capex lines only by assertion (capex_other 0.0 default).
challenges.answer: The North Kalimantan power spend is not a development project held outside the balance sheet: the capex was absorbed to the nine-month mark of FY2025 (F7/S13), before the 30 June 2026 balance-sheet date, so it is already inside the reported property, plant and equipment and its funding is inside the modelled capex line (capex_unit reconciles to the US$250-300m annual programme, S13). The annual report's segment note shows the electricity-rental segment carrying essentially no external revenue (S15), so it earns nothing in the model - a bridge add-back of US$243m would add cash already inside the balance sheet a second time and would double count the capex that the FCFF already debits.

missing_bull_case.note: Two sourced upsides are absent from value: the up-to-US$550m contingent Kestrel consideration (F13/S6) is carried at zero with no probability sizing attempt, and the deck's own flatter HBA path (reviewed, spot 126.8 easing to LT) is not quantified against the steeper Newcastle path the model prices off, even as a stated value-per-dollar sensitivity.

missing_bear_case.note: The bear shocks price, volume and one cost residual but never tests the reserve-boundary overdraw (863 Mt window vs ~839 Mt ex-Kestrel base), an IUPK extension refusal past 1 Oct 2032 (F19/S15), or the receivables divergence the report itself flags as optics-class, each named in §3/§6.

conservatism_audit.note: Optimistic-side departures without sources: (1) FY2025A sales 71.94 Mt vs FY2025 revenue-implied ~68.7 Mt inflates first-year revenue ~US$180m; (2) 14.2% flat royalty vs 18% band plus 10% profit-share understates state take ~9pp; (3) 12y window draws 863 Mt vs ~839 Mt base; (4) payout decay 85% to 55% vs LK 26%; (5) zero value for 243m sunk power capex (S13). flags.justification: The FY2026E payout step-up is the Kestrel-proceeds distribution management committed the cash to — S2 reports the proceeds are earmarked "untuk ekspansi domestik, dividen dan pembayaran sebagian utang grup" [S2] — and it is anchored on a DEMONSTRATED payout, not on the FY2025 26% [S15]: FY2024 dividends declared EXCEEDED parent net profit, and FY2025 is itself a transition year (no Kestrel gain, price trough), so its low ratio is not the normal level. The decay is not a cautious haircut and the level is not unsourced: it restates the LK's own paid history, and the payout carries zero method weight in the primary life-of-asset DCF (weights dcf_life 0.85 / ev_ebitda 0.15 / div_yield 0.0), so it cannot move the target down.

The owner's V5.1 diagnosis names the statutory band over a 14.2%-paid cost base as the mixed convention this refresh corrects, and the engine's calibration gate (FY2025A EBITDA reproduced to -1.5%) structurally holds that convention. IUPK is stated as params.licence with its source (S15/F19); the 18% band and the 4%+6% net-profit shares under Article 16(1)e/i [S14] are disclosed in the report as the state-take risk, and the FY2024 comparative take of 19.98% (F21) is carried in the report beside it.

flags.justification: The house COAL default weights are dcf_life 0.6 / ev_ebitda 0.25 / div_yield 0.15. We weight the life-DCF at 0.85 and the peer-median EV/EBITDA cross-check at 0.15, and drop the dividend-yield method to zero, because its capitalisation rate is the peer median and most of the comp set pays no dividend [S0], so the median collapses and capitalises the dividend at a nonsense multiple; the anchor itself is disclosed in §4. The primary method is the house method card's through-cycle life-of-asset DCF [S15].
